notes.meaning: Paul begins answering questions the Corinthians had sent him about spiritual gifts, which are special abilities given by the Holy Spirit. He does not want believers to stay confused or misinformed about how these gifts work. God gave these gifts to build up the church, not to stir up rivalry or pride.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christians frequently received these gifts of the Spirit through the sacraments of baptism and confirmation.

notes.meaning: Paul reminds the believers of their past life before they came to faith in Christ. Back then, they were led astray into worshiping idols that could neither hear nor speak. In contrast to those lifeless statues, the true and living God actually speaks and works through His people.

Paul offers a basic test to tell whether someone is truly guided by God's Spirit. A person speaking by the Holy Spirit will never curse Jesus, because the Spirit always honors Him. Sincere confession that Jesus is Lord can only come through the work of the Holy Spirit in a person's life.

Paul shows how the three Persons of the Trinity work together in the church. There are different spiritual gifts from the same Holy Spirit, different ways to serve under the same Lord Jesus, and different results produced by the same God the Father. God provides great variety, but all true gifts come from one unified divine source.

Every believer receives a visible working of the Holy Spirit in some way. God does not give these gifts so people can boast or feel superior to others. Instead, the Spirit gives them for the common good, so that the whole church family is helped and strengthened.

Paul lists several sample gifts the Spirit gives to different believers. These include words of wisdom and knowledge, extraordinary faith, gifts of healing, miraculous powers, prophecy, the ability to tell true spirits from false ones, speaking in unknown languages, and interpreting those languages. God distributes these varied abilities so the church has everything it needs to carry out His work.

differ.view: Pentecostals teach that all the gifts in this list, including miracles, prophecy, and tongues, are supernatural powers that the Holy Spirit still gives to Christians today. In church worship, they believe speaking in tongues should be followed by an interpretation so that everyone present can understand and be built up in their faith.

Historic Reformed churches teach that miraculous gifts like tongues, prophecy, and miracles were temporary "sign gifts" given only during the time of the early apostles to help establish the church. Because the Bible is now complete, they believe these extraordinary signs have ceased (stopped), and the Spirit now works through Bible preaching, prayer, and the sacraments (sacred practices like Baptism and the Lord’s Supper).

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Because the church continues across the centuries as Christ's living body, the gifts and ministries listed here also continue under the guidance of church shepherds.

notes.meaning: The Holy Spirit Himself is the active power behind all these abilities. He decides who receives each gift according to His own wise purpose, rather than human ambition. Believers can be content with their calling, knowing God chose what was best for them.

Paul compares the church to a human body. A person's body is a single unit made of many different parts, like hands, feet, and eyes. In the exact same way, all believers together make up the one body of Christ.

Every believer has been united into this single body by the Holy Spirit. Earthly barriers like race, culture, or social rank no longer divide Christians, because all have been given the same Spirit to share. Christians are joined together as one spiritual family at conversion.

differ.view: The Assemblies of God teaches that the Holy Spirit is the one doing the baptizing here, placing a person into Christ's body at conversion (when someone first turns to Jesus in faith). They distinguish this from "baptism in the Holy Spirit," which they see as a separate, later gift where Jesus baptizes the believer to give them special power for ministry.

The Orthodox Presbyterian Church teaches that every true Christian is baptized by the Holy Spirit into the church the moment they are saved. Because all believers already share this gift, they believe Christians do not need to seek a "second blessing" (a separate spiritual experience later on) to receive the Spirit.

notes.meaning: A human body does not consist of just one large part, but of many different parts. In the same way, the church cannot exist if everyone has the same gifts and roles. Variety is necessary for the whole body to live and work properly.

Paul pictures a foot wishing it were a hand, or an ear wishing it were an eye. Comparing oneself to another and feeling less important does not remove a person from the body. Every believer belongs in the church, even if their gifts seem less prominent.

If the whole body were only an eye, a person would have no way to hear sounds. If the entire body were an ear, there would be no sense of smell. A church would become completely useless if every member were identical.

God personally arranged every limb and organ in the physical body exactly where He wanted it. In the very same way, God places every believer into the church according to His own perfect design. We can trust that God knows where each of us fits best.

If every part were the same, there would be no complete body at all. Instead, God made many distinct members that work together as one whole unit. The strength of the church lies in its diverse members being united in Christ.

More prominent parts of the body cannot look down on quieter parts. The eye cannot tell the hand it is unneeded, and the head cannot dismiss the feet. In the church, leaders and gifted speakers still rely entirely on the daily help of other members.

Parts of the body that seem delicate or weaker, like inner organs, are actually the most essential for life. In daily life, people take special care to clothe and protect parts of the body that seem less presentable. God arranged the body this way so that extra honor goes to the parts that seem to lack it, showing that quieter Christians are deeply valued by Him.

God designed the body with diverse parts so there would be no conflict or division among them. Instead, every part is meant to care equally for the others. When one part hurts, the whole body feels the pain, and when one part is honored, every part shares in the joy.

Paul applies his word picture directly to the believers in Corinth. Together they make up the body of Christ, and each individual person is an essential member of it. Every Christian has a unique place and purpose within the church family.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Paul describes an organized, visible church body headed by authorized offices, which supports the principle of apostolic succession.

notes.meaning: God established specific offices and gifts to help the church flourish. First are apostles sent with Christ's authority, second are prophets who speak God's truth, and third are teachers who instruct others. God also provided miracles, gifts of healing, helping the needy, leadership skills, and different kinds of tongues.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The list presents an order of dignity where teaching ranks above miracles and tongues, while 'helps' and 'governments' refer to ordained offices like deacons and priests.

notes.meaning: Paul asks a series of questions that all expect the answer, 'No, of course not.' Not everyone is an apostle, prophet, or teacher, and not everyone performs miracles or speaks in tongues. God spreads different gifts among different people rather than giving every gift to everyone.

differ.view: Speaking in tongues was never intended for every believer, so it cannot be required as proof of being filled with the Spirit.
Paul is addressing the public gift of tongues used in church assemblies, which is distinct from praying in tongues as the initial sign of the baptism in the Holy Spirit available to all.

notes.meaning: Paul encourages believers to earnestly desire the gifts that do the most to build up the church. Even so, he promises to show them a way to live that is far better than merely possessing great abilities. This sets the stage for his famous teaching on Christian love.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Love is the supreme gift and virtue that gives true value to every other gift and outlasts them all.
